---
title: "Predicting food webs: the allometric diet breadth model"
author: "Owen Petchey"
date: 2026-09-14
categories: [research, food webs, allometric diet breadth model]
image: cover.jpg
---

A food web is the network of who eats whom in a community, and for decades ecologists mostly had to observe or guess at that network species pair by species pair. The allometric diet breadth model (ADBM) takes a different approach: it predicts a predator's diet — and so an entire food web's structure — from body sizes alone.

The idea builds on optimal foraging theory: a predator should include a prey species in its diet if doing so increases its net rate of energy intake, and both the profitability of an attack and the risk of it succeeding scale predictably with the body sizes of predator and prey. Given nothing more than a list of species' body sizes, the ADBM ranks potential prey by profitability and predicts which a predator should and shouldn't eat, generating a whole predicted food web that can be compared against real, observed ones.

The model was introduced in [Beckerman, Petchey & Warren (2006), "Foraging biology predicts food web complexity"](https://www.pnas.org/content/103/37/13745), and has since been used and extended by the group and others to ask how far body size alone can take us in predicting community structure. It connects directly to the group's [broader history of food web research](../2019-03-04-food-webs-history/index.qmd) and to the [R tools](../2019-03-04-food-web-tools/index.qmd) used to build and analyse these predicted webs.
